reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

reading.ours: collection.upsertEntity(row) — a key this population has never seen
reading.caveat: THE FLOOR DOES LESS, AND KNOWABLY SO. Ours mints an identity (a slot and an entry in the identity store — there is no per-index `links` cell, so a row carries nothing per index at all), copies the row, walks the copy's own names to refuse the ones a row may not carry, stamps the slot, stamps the collection and records the row on the presence channel so every index and every whole-population reader hears about it. The floor allocates one copy and hashes one string. Direction: this inflates our ratio, and no three-line floor can close the gap — what the extra buys is that anything subscribed to this population, or indexing it, is woken by this insert. The tracked row below is the closest a few lines get. Both sides abandon their container between passes and both are collected outside the clock, so the GC of what each allocated is NOT inside either number; our allocation per row is roughly three objects to the floor's one, and that debt is paid later.

reading.caveat: THE FAIRER FLOOR, and it is still not equal. The floor now keeps a per-row frame stamp and a queue, so something downstream could be told — which is the job our insert is doing and the bare Map is not. What the floor still does not have: an identity that outlives the value, a per-index cell on every row, a presence channel that tells indexes and whole-population readers separately from the row itself, or any means of recording WHICH columns moved. THAT DEFAULT IS SAMEVALUEZERO AND WAS AN INLINE `===` WHEN 2026-08-20-price/write WAS RECORDED. The call was there under both — the predicate has always been reached through the strategy's captured parameter — so the delta is one comparison, and only on a column that moved, which is one per write here. `update.column-vs-the-strict-equality-default` is that delta on its own and is unrun; until it runs, this row's recorded figure is a figure for the older body. Direction: inflates our ratio; the tracked row below prices the part of that a person would have had to write anyway. The patch object is REUSED rather than written as a literal per call — a caller who writes { title } inline pays one more allocation per write than this row charges us for. The batch closes with one flush per eight thousand writes, which is why every write in it takes the marking path rather than the already-stamped early return. THE REUSED PATCH IS ALSO WHAT STOPS THIS ROW BEING SUBTRACTED FROM `update.unchanged-vs-field-store`, and that subtraction is the only way anyone has to split this number into the walk that decides and the tail that reports. reading.caveat: THE ROW ABOVE, ARM FOR ARM WITH `update.unchanged-vs-field-store`, AND THAT IS ITS WHOLE REASON. The only handle anybody has on how the row above's gap divides is the unchanged row, which times the same call up to the point where the comparator finds every column equal and returns before marking anything. Subtracting one from the other would give the walk and the tail — except that the two bodies differ in three ways at once: the row above REUSES one patch object where the unchanged row allocates eight thousand and hands a different one to every write, and its floor stores a local where the unchanged row's floor reads the value off the patch first. A fresh patch per write is a fresh receiver for `isPlain` and for the `for…in`, and the extra load is a real instruction on the floor. Both differences push the same way and neither is the thing being priced. THIS ROW REMOVES ALL THREE. The patch supply is the unchanged row's — one object per row, built outside the clock — and the floor is the unchanged row's floor to the character. What is left between this row's `ours` and the unchanged row's `ours` is exactly what a write that MOVES a column does and a write that moves nothing does not: one store into the entity, the moved-names array and its push, two `channel.write` calls — the row and the population — one `columnSlotStoreService.get` probe for the moved column inside `OIMColumnOwner.markColumnsChanged`, and the frame that closes the batch. EIGHT PATCH ARRAYS, ONE PER TITLE, so this row moves the column on exactly the writes the row above moves it on. The title advances by one of eight per batch and every row in a batch is written with the same title, which is the row above's rotation with the shared object unpicked into one object per row. THE FLUSH IS ON THIS SIDE OF THE SUBTRACTION AND NOT ON THE UNCHANGED ROW'S: nothing is marked there, so no frame is asked for. `flush.empty-vs-noop` [2026-08-20-price/frame] prices a frame with nothing queued, and over eight thousand writes it is four thousandths of a nanosecond each — named here because it belongs to the difference, not because it can be seen in it.

reading.floor: test the row for a column store and the population for listeners, then row.title = value
reading.caveat: THE TWO "IS ANYBODY LISTENING" GUARDS, PUT ON THE FLOOR. A write that moves a column asks two questions before it can skip the routing: `OIMColumnOwner.markColumnsChanged` tests `carrierSlot.columnSlotStore === undefined` (no column of this row was ever subscribed to), and `OIMSlotAggregate.contentChanged` tests `listeners.length === 0` (no index hears this population). OUR ARM IS THAT ROW'S ARM TO THE CHARACTER — the same fixture, the same reused patch, the same rotation of eight titles, the same flush per eight thousand writes. OPERATION COUNT, THE DIFFERENCE ONLY: one field load and one `undefined` compare per row, one length load and one compare per row. Expected inside the noise floor.

reading.ours: collection.updateEntity(slot, patch) — the shipped default, which is SameValueZero
reading.floor: the same update on a population built with createOIMEntityWriterInPlace({ sameValueGuard: (a, b) => a === b })
reading.caveat: THE ONE ITEM OF THE WRITE PATH THAT IS IN NO RECORDED NUMBER, BECAUSE IT POSTDATES THEM ALL. Every write row in `2026-08-20-price/write` was measured against a default equality that was an inline `a === b`. The default is `oimSameValueZeroGuard` now — `a === b || (a !== a && b !== b)` — and what that costs is not a call, since the predicate was already reached through the strategy's captured parameter on both designs. IT IS ONE COMPARISON, AND ONLY ON A COLUMN THAT MOVED: an equal column settles on the first clause and short-circuits, byte for byte what was there before, while a moved column then evaluates `a !== a` and short-circuits on that. BOTH ARMS ARE `collection.update` ON THE SAME FIXTURE, one column moving per write, so the difference is that one comparison per write and the state of one inline cache. The floor's predicate is a different function object of the same shape as the shipped `oimSameValueZeroGuard` — module-level, monomorphic, one expression, no closure. THIS PAIR DECLARES `isolate` AND IT MUST. `changedColumns` is ONE compiled body however many writers the factory builds, so `sameValueGuard(entity[name], source[name])` inside it is one call site for the whole process. Building both arms in one process would make that site see two functions and would spoil BOTH of them equally, which is a measurement of nothing. The same reasoning, and the same declaration, is on `alt.equality-predicate.shared-default-vs-inlined.with-a-second-comparator-present`, where making the site polymorphic is the subject rather than the hazard. DO NOT BORROW `alt.equality-predicate.shared-default-vs-inlined.unchanged-resend` FOR THIS. That row prices the predicate's CALL FRAME against a walk with no parameter at all, on an UNCHANGED re-send where every column settles on the first clause — so the second comparison this row exists for never executes in it. The two rows are about the parameter and about the body, and they do not substitute. ONE COMPARISON PER WRITE IS BELOW WHAT THIS INSTRUMENT RESOLVED ON ITS OWN SCALE CONTROL, and that is the expected reading, stated in advance so a run can refute it: this pair should come back inside the noise floor. If it does, the argument in `oimSameValueZeroGuard.ts` — that the new answer is free on the hot path and spends only where it saves a report, a reindex and a wake-up — holds at the write. If it does NOT, there is a real cost on the hottest path in the engine and the `NaN` defect was bought with something.

reading.ours: collection.updateEntity(slot, patch) — one column, no index reads it
reading.floor: gate on !==, stamp the row once per frame, queue it, store
reading.caveat: THE FLOOR NOW DOES THE JOB. It compares before it writes, so a re-send moves nothing; it stamps the row with the frame number so ten writes to one row queue it once; and it queues the row so a frame could deliver it. Four lines. What it still does not do: record WHICH columns moved (so no field-granular subscription is possible), route to an index, or mark the collection separately from the row. Direction: still inflates our ratio, and this is the number to quote when somebody asks what the engine costs over doing it properly by hand.

reading.ours: collection.updateEntity(slot, patch) with the value the row already holds
reading.floor: row.title = value — a store that always happens
reading.caveat: THE TWO SIDES DO OPPOSITE THINGS, ON PURPOSE. Ours walks the patch, finds every column equal, returns before marking anything and wakes nobody; the floor stores unconditionally because it has nothing to protect. So this is not "which is faster at the same work" — it is what the comparator gate costs when it fires, against the cheapest possible thing that ignores the question. No flush closes this batch, because nothing was marked and there is nothing for a frame to deliver: that is the point of the row. Direction: inflates our ratio; what the gate buys is that a screen re-sending a server payload it already holds does not repaint.

reading.floor: const row = map.get(id); if (row !== undefined) row.title = value
reading.caveat: THE ONE WRITE ROW WHERE BOTH SIDES PAY THE LOOKUP, which is what makes it the fair comparison for a key that arrived from outside. Ours is one map read and then the identity path priced two rows up; the floor is one map read and a store. The difference between this ratio and the update.column ratio is the price of NOT having held the identity — the engine's own source puts that at 103-132 ns against 36-51 [NO RUN BEHIND THIS FIGURE], and this row is the independent check on that claim.

reading.ours: collection.upsertEntity(row) — a key that already carries a value
reading.floor: copy five columns onto the stored object, one store each
reading.caveat: THE FLOOR CANNOT EXPRESS ONE HALF OF WHAT UPSERT PROMISES. An upsert of an existing key also REMOVES the columns the new value does not carry, which means walking the stored row to find them; here both rows carry all five columns, so that walk finds nothing and the floor's five stores are the same net effect. Ours additionally gates each column on the default equality, so only the column that actually moved is written and reported, where the floor writes all five every time. THAT DEFAULT IS SAMEVALUEZERO AND WAS AN INLINE `===` WHEN THIS ROW WAS RECORDED: the four columns this fixture does not move settle on the first clause and cost what they cost before, and the one that moves carries one comparison this figure never saw. Direction: mixed — the gate saves us four stores and costs us five comparisons plus a moved-list allocation, and the marking and routing are ours alone. Read it beside update.column: the difference between the two is what sending a whole row costs over sending the column that changed. THE STRUCTURAL CAVEAT AT THE HEAD OF THIS REPORT RUNS BACKWARDS ON THIS ROW AND ON NO OTHER WRITE ROW. It says a Map-keyed floor pays a hash our identity path does not, which flatters us. Here it is the reverse: the floor is handed `held[i]` by its index and never looks anything up, while ours is handed a ROW and must resolve its key — `keyOf` and then the store lookup inside `writeContentByKey`, a `Map.get` over eight thousand string keys. That lookup is inside our number and outside the floor's, so this row overstates what the design costs a caller who already holds the identity. `upsert.whole-row-vs-map-get-and-five-stores` is the same measurement with the lookup on both sides; the difference between the two rows is the hash, and neither alone is the price of an upsert.

reading.ours: collection.upsertEntity(row) — a key that already carries a value
reading.floor: const stored = map.get(row.id); then copy five columns onto it
reading.caveat: THE ROW ABOVE, WITH THE LOOKUP PUT BACK ON THE FLOOR. `upsertEntity` is handed a ROW and not an identity, so it calls `keyOf` and then `writeContentByKey` — a `Map.get` over eight thousand string keys — before it can write anything. The floor of `upsert.whole-row-vs-five-stores` is handed `held[i]` by its loop index and never looks anything up, which makes that row the one write row in this suite where the hash falls on OUR side. Here the floor resolves the same key through its own `Map` first, so both sides pay one hash and the row is what a person doing this job by hand would actually have written. OUR SIDE IS THE SAME BODY AS THE ROW ABOVE, deliberately and to the line: the same fixture, the same two whole-row variants alternating so the title moves on every row of every pass, the same flush per eight thousand writes. Nothing about our arm differs, so the two rows' `ours` columns should agree to within the between-pair disagreement of this piece, and the difference between the two FLOORS is one `Map.get` and one `undefined` test. READ THE PAIR OF ROWS, NOT EITHER ONE: the row above prices an upsert against a floor that already knows where the row is, this one against a floor that has to find out, and a caller sits at one or the other depending on whether the write came from a socket payload or from something they were holding. WHAT IS STILL NOT EQUAL. The floor's five stores are unconditional where ours gates each column on the default equality — SameValueZero — and writes the one that moved; ours walks the stored row for columns the new value does not carry (here it finds none, so the net effect matches); and the marking, the presence of a `columnSlotStoreService.get` probe per moved column and the frame that closes the batch are ours alone. All three are stated on the row above and are unchanged by moving the lookup — this row changes exactly one thing about that comparison, which is the point of it.

reading.ours: collection.upsertEntity(row) — a key that already carries a value
reading.floor: walk the stored row for columns the new one does not carry, then five stores
reading.caveat: THE DEPARTURE WALK, PUT ON THE FLOOR, WHICH IS THE ONLY WAY THIS HARNESS CAN PRICE AN OPERATION THAT NEITHER ARM OF AN EXISTING ROW ISOLATES. `upsert.whole-row-vs-five-stores` charges our side a walk of the STORED row's own names, with a `hasOwnProperty` probe of the caller's row per name, and its floor makes neither — so the walk sits inside that row's residual with the marking, the routing and four extra columns of comparison, and nothing separates it from them. Here the floor makes the identical walk, to the line of `OIMEntityCollection.writeEntity`, and stores five columns after it. THE ITEM IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THIS ROW'S GAP AND THAT ROW'S GAP, and nothing else about either arm changes. OUR ARM IS THAT ROW'S ARM TO THE CHARACTER — the same fixture, the same two whole-row variants alternating so `title` moves on every row of every pass, the same flush per eight thousand writes, the same absence of an index, a subscriber and a projection. So the two rows' `ours` columns should agree to within the between-pair disagreement of this piece, and a run where they do not is a run that has said something about the machine rather than about the walk. OPERATION COUNT, THE DIFFERENCE ONLY: one `for…in` over the five names the stored row carries, five `hasOwnProperty` probes of a five-property row, and one `??=` test that never fires — both rows of this fixture carry all five columns, so nothing ever leaves and no array is allocated on either arm. That is the walk at its CHEAPEST: it finds nothing, which is what a server re-sending whole rows always makes it do, and it is the case an upsert being a whole-row replace is charged for. A payload that genuinely drops a column would add a push, a `deleteColumns` call and an `undefined` write per departing name to our side and a `delete` to the floor. WHAT THIS ROW IS NOT. It is not a merge-versus-replace comparison — the floor here is not the rejected design, it is the shipped design with one item lifted out of it and set beside a hand-written store. The rejected design is `upsertEntity` WITHOUT the walk, which is `upsert.whole-row-vs-five-stores` with a floor that does less, and no row in this suite is that. Read this one as the price of the item, not as a verdict on the consequence.

Both arms write the same number of rows through the same depth over three populations round-robin, and DIFFER ONLY IN HOW MANY CLASSES stand at that one call site: three, or one constructed three times. The three classes have IDENTICAL BODIES — they are written out separately rather than generated, because a factory hands back one class and that is the other arm. WHAT IT DECIDES: whether a consumer may freely mix layer types, or whether a layer API should be one class parameterised by a callback. In that stored run that is 402432 updates performed against 400514 charged on our side and 626688 against 625872 on the floor, which moves that stored ratio by less than one part in two hundred. THE OVERSHOOT WAS A FALSE COUNT, IT IS GONE, AND IT WAS NOT WHAT AILS THIS ROW.
